# PCB-to-chip transition: EMerge (FEM)

[EMerge](https://github.com/FennisRobert/EMerge) simulation of the OTTER benchmark: an FR4
board, three gold bondwires and the top metal stack of an IHP SG13G2 chip, 1–30 GHz. The
geometry is imported as one STEP file per object, as exported from FreeCAD.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This script needs **EMerge 3.0** (we used the pre-release **3.0.0a6**) because it uses
> **`sim.set_scale_factor(1000)`**. Without the scaling, the micrometre-sized chip parts
> trip up gmsh and OpenCASCADE. See [the scaling issue](#the-scaling-issue-and-how-it-was-solved).

## Result

| | \|S11\| error vs CST, RMS / max (1–30 GHz) | S21 notch |
|---|---|---|
| **EMerge (this script)** | **0.99 / 2.65 dB** | 27.00 GHz, −25.9 dB |
| openEMS, all metals PEC | 0.95 / 2.68 dB | 27.00 GHz, −29.2 dB |
| CST (reference) | – | 28.53 GHz, −28.2 dB |

EMerge agrees with openEMS when both use PEC metals. The gap to CST comes mainly from the
material model: in this script the PCB copper and the chip metals are PEC. With lossy copper
and chip metals, openEMS moves the notch to 28.5 GHz.

## Folder contents

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `emerge_simulation.py` | The simulation script |
| `step_files/` | One STEP file per object, exported from FreeCAD (mm) |

## EMerge version

| | |
|---|---|
| Required | **EMerge 3.0.x** (pre-release) |
| Used for the benchmark | **3.0.0a6** (supports Python 3.10–3.13) |
| Not working | EMerge 2.8.5 and older: they have no `set_scale_factor()` |

```bash
python3 -m venv ~/venv_emerge
source ~/venv_emerge/bin/activate
pip install emerge==3.0.0a6
```

The script calls `sim.check_version("3.0.0")`. This stops the run with a `VersionError` if
the installed EMerge has a different major.minor version (for example 2.8 or 3.1), so the
script never runs on a version it was not written for.

## The scaling issue and how it was solved

**The problem.** EMerge models in metres by default. The chip parts are tiny: Metal5 is
0.49 µm thick (4.9e-7 m), port 1 is 8 × 5.65 µm and the bondwires are 30 µm in diameter.
In metres these sizes come close to the geometric tolerance of OpenCASCADE (1e-7), which
EMerge uses through gmsh for the STEP import, the boolean operations and the meshing. These
tiny structures trip up gmsh and OpenCASCADE.

**The first workaround (EMerge 2.8.5).** Every length was scaled up by hand (`mm = 1.0`
instead of `0.001`), and the frequencies were scaled down by 1000 (MHz instead of GHz)
while meshing, so that the mesh kept the right size relative to the wavelength. After
meshing, EMerge's internal mesh arrays (nodes, edge lengths, areas, volumes) were divided by
1000 by hand and the frequencies were set back to GHz. This depends on EMerge internals and
is easy to get wrong.

**The solution (EMerge 3.0).** `sim.set_scale_factor(1000)` builds and meshes the model
1000× larger, then scales the mesh back by 1/1000 before solving. The script defines its
units for this scale:

```python
mm = 0.001*1000    # = 1.0   (1 mm is 1 model unit)
um = 1e-6*1000     # = 1e-3
nm = 1e-9*1000     # = 1e-6

sim = em.Simulation("04_simple", save_file=True, loglevel='INFO')
sim.check_version("3.0.0")
sim.set_scale_factor(1000)
```

The smallest feature, 0.49 µm, becomes 4.9e-4 model units, far above the tolerance.
Frequencies stay in real Hz. EMerge prints a warning that global scaling is an experimental
feature; this is expected.

**Units to use with the scaling:**

| Quantity | Units | In the script |
|---|---|---|
| Geometry: STEP import, port plates | Scaled (×1000): use `mm`, `um`, or `s = 1000` | `STEPItems(..., unit=mm)`, `p1_start = [-2.9e-3*s, ...]` |
| Mesh sizes, open-region margins | Scaled | `set_size(obj, 0.1*mm)`, `open_region(1, 1, 1)` = 1 mm |
| Frequencies | Real Hz | `set_frequency_range(1e9, 30e9, 50)` |
| Lumped-port width and height | **Real metres** (divide by `s`) | `LumpedPort(port_in, 1, width=h1/s, height=th1/s, ...)` |

> [!NOTE]
> Scripts generated by the OTTER add-on use the same scaling when **Grid Settings → Solver
> mesh (global) → geometry scale factor** is set to 1000 (default 1 = metres).

## How to run

```bash
source ~/venv_emerge/bin/activate
cd examples/pcb_to_chip/emerge
SHOW_PLOTS=0 EMERGE_THREADS=16 python3 emerge_simulation.py
```

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `SHOW_PLOTS` | `1` | `0` = no 3D views of the model and mesh and no plot windows (servers, batch runs) |
| `EMERGE_THREADS` | all cores | Number of solver threads |

## Output

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `results/04_simple_Sparams.csv` | **The result:** frequency (Hz), S11 and S21 as real, imaginary, dB and degrees |
| `results/04_simple_Sparams.png` | Magnitude and phase of S11 and S21 |
| `04_simple.EMResults/` | EMerge's saved simulation data (`save_file=True`); can be several hundred MB |

The curve in `results/EMerge/Sparameters.csv` at the repository root uses the same 129
frequency points as openEMS (100 Hz – 30 GHz), so its sweep differed from this script.

## Main settings

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Frequency sweep | 1–30 GHz, 50 points |
| Mesh resolution | `set_resolution(0.33)`: fraction of the wavelength, lower = finer |
| Curved surfaces | `set_curved_boundary_meshing(6)` |
| Element sizes | Bondwires 0.1 mm, PCB 0.25 mm, chip metals 100 µm, SiO2 10 µm, air 2 mm, port faces width/5 |
| Air region | `open_region(1, 1, 1)`: 1 mm of air beyond the structure's bounding box on each side, absorbing boundary on its outer faces |
| Ports | Lumped, 50 Ω, along z. Port 1 at the chip edge (8 × 5.65 µm), excited; port 2 at the board edge (500 × 254 µm) |
| Materials | FR4 εr = 4.3, SiO2 εr = 4.1, bondwires gold 4.561e7 S/m; PCB copper and chip metals PEC |
| Mesher | `safe_mode = True` |

## Next steps

These checks follow from the openEMS and Palace findings and have not been run in EMerge yet:

1. Lossy PCB copper (5.8e7 S/m) and the chip-metal conductivities of the SG13G2 stack-up.
   In openEMS this moved the notch from 27.0 to 28.5 GHz.
2. A larger air region: 1 mm is less than λ/4 at 30 GHz (2.5 mm). Palace needed 3 mm.
3. A fine mesh in the air inside the bondwire loops (Palace V5 uses 25 µm), then refining
   until the notch frequency changes by less than 0.2 GHz.
4. A finer frequency step around 26–30 GHz to resolve the notch depth.
